records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֧ח יְהוָ֛ה אֶת־נָתָ֖ן אֶל־דָּוִ֑ד וַיָּבֹ֣א אֵלָ֗יו וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לוֹ֙ שְׁנֵ֣י אֲנָשִׁ֗ים הָיוּ֙ בְּעִ֣יר אֶחָ֔ת אֶחָ֥ד עָשִׁ֖יר וְאֶחָ֥ד רָֽאשׁ׃
records.gloss: And sent Yahweh Nathan to David, and he came to him and said to him, two men were in city one, one rich and one poor.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said, "In a certain city there were two men, one of them rich and the other poor.

L.1: And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} sent Nathan to David. And he came to him and said to him, "There were two men in one city, one rich and the other poor.

R.1: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} sent Nathan to David. Nathan came to him and said, "Two men lived in a town. One was rich, and the other was poor.

decisions.choice: the LORD sent Nathan: God answers what David did in chapter 11
decisions.reason: The last words of chapter 11 were that what David had done was evil in Yahweh's eyes (11:27). Now Yahweh acts. Nathan is the prophet who brought David the promise of a lasting house (7:2-17); he now brings God's judgment.

decisions.choice: two men: a story told as a case for the king to judge
decisions.reason: Nathan does not say at first that this is a parable. He tells it like a real complaint brought to the king, who was the highest judge in the land (15:2-4). David is meant to give his verdict before he sees that the case is about himself. A wise woman uses the same method in 14:4-11, and a prophet in 1 Kings 20:39-41.

decisions.choice: poor: a man with little or nothing
decisions.reason: The word describes someone without property or means (Proverbs 13:23; 1 Samuel 18:23, where David calls himself "a poor man"). It sets up the contrast with the rich man's many flocks.

decisions.choice: Nathan came to him
decisions.reason: Readable names Nathan, where the Hebrew says only "he", so that the reader does not take the subject to be David.

records.heading: Nathan confronts David

records.source: לְעָשִׁ֗יר הָיָ֛ה צֹ֥אן וּבָקָ֖ר הַרְבֵּ֥ה מְאֹֽד׃
records.gloss: To [the] rich [man] were flocks and herds many very.
pieces: The rich man had a great many sheep and cattle.

L.2: The rich [man] had very many flocks and herds.

R.2: The rich man had very large flocks of sheep and herds of cattle.

decisions.choice: flocks and herds: sheep and goats, and cattle
decisions.reason: The first word covers small livestock, sheep and goats together; the second covers cattle. Together they sum up a herdsman's wealth (Genesis 13:5; 1 Samuel 27:9).

decisions.choice: sheep and cattle (Balanced); flocks of sheep and herds of cattle (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the animals, since "flocks and herds" is less familiar. Readable keeps "flocks" and "herds" and says what they were made up of.

records.source: וְלָרָ֣שׁ אֵֽין־כֹּ֗ל כִּי֩ אִם־כִּבְשָׂ֨ה אַחַ֤ת קְטַנָּה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר קָנָ֔ה וַיְחַיֶּ֕הָ וַתִּגְדַּ֥ל עִמּ֛וֹ וְעִם־בָּנָ֖יו יַחְדָּ֑ו מִפִּתּ֨וֹ תֹאכַ֜ל וּמִכֹּס֤וֹ תִשְׁתֶּה֙ וּבְחֵיק֣וֹ תִשְׁכָּ֔ב וַתְּהִי־ל֖וֹ כְּבַֽת׃
records.gloss: And to the poor [man] there was not anything except ewe-lamb one small which he had bought, and he kept her alive, and she grew up with him and with his sons together; from his morsel she would eat, and from his cup she would drink, and in his bosom she would lie, and she was to him like a daughter.
pieces: But the poor man had nothing except one little ewe lamb that he had bought. He nurtured it, and it grew up with him alongside his {{gender:children|sons}}. It shared his bit of bread, drank from his cup and lay in his arms; it was like a daughter to him.

L.3: But the poor [man] had nothing except one little ewe lamb, which he had bought. And he kept it alive, and it grew up with him and with his {{gender:children|sons}} together. It would eat from his morsel and drink from his cup and lie in his bosom, and it was like a daughter to him.

R.3: But the poor man had nothing except one little female lamb that he had bought. He took care of it, and it grew up in his home together with his {{gender:children|sons}}. It ate from his plate and drank from his cup, and it even slept in his arms. The lamb was like a daughter to him.

decisions.choice: one little ewe lamb: a single animal kept as part of the family
decisions.reason: A poor household might own one lamb and raise it by hand. This one is treated like a child of the house: it eats the man's own food and sleeps in his arms. Its loss is the loss of something loved, not only of property.

decisions.choice: would eat, would drink, would lie: what happened day after day
decisions.reason: The verb forms describe the lamb's daily life with the family, not a single meal.

decisions.choice: lay in his bosom ... like a daughter: words that point toward the real case
decisions.reason: "Bosom" is the word for a close embrace, used of a wife in verse 8 and in Deuteronomy 13:7; 28:54. The lamb is "like a daughter" (Hebrew *bat*), and the woman in chapter 11 is Bathsheba, whose name begins with the same word. The story is told so that David can hear it as being about a man's beloved, though he does not yet see it.

decisions.choice: his sons: his children
decisions.reason: The plural of "son" often covers a man's children of both sexes. Nothing in the story limits it to boys.

decisions.choice: shared his bit of bread, lay in his arms (Balanced); ate from his plate, slept in his arms (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Morsel" is a piece of bread, a share of the man's own meal; Readable says "ate from his plate". "Bosom" becomes "arms". Readable adds "even" to show that this is the most striking detail.

records.source: וַיָּ֣בֹא הֵלֶךְ֮ לְאִ֣ישׁ הֶֽעָשִׁיר֒ וַיַּחְמֹ֗ל לָקַ֤חַת מִצֹּאנוֹ֙ וּמִבְּקָר֔וֹ לַעֲשׂ֕וֹת לָאֹרֵ֖חַ הַבָּא־ל֑וֹ וַיִּקַּ֗ח אֶת־כִּבְשַׂת֙ הָאִ֣ישׁ הָרָ֔אשׁ וַֽיַּעֲשֶׂ֔הָ לָאִ֖ישׁ הַבָּ֥א אֵלָֽיו׃
records.gloss: And came a traveler to [the] man the rich, and he spared to take from his flock and from his herd to prepare for the wayfarer who had come to him; and he took [the] ewe-lamb of the man the poor and prepared it for the man who had come to him.
pieces: Then a traveler came to the rich man. He did not want to take one of his own sheep or cattle to prepare for the visitor who had come to him. So he took the poor man's ewe lamb and prepared it for his guest."

L.4: And a traveler came to the rich man, and he spared taking from his own flock and from his own herd to prepare for the wayfarer who had come to him. And he took the poor man's ewe lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him."

R.4: One day a traveler came to visit the rich man. The rich man did not want to kill any of his own sheep or cattle to make a meal for his guest. So he took the poor man's lamb and cooked it for the visitor."

decisions.choice: he spared: he was unwilling to part with his own animals
decisions.reason: The verb means to feel pity for something and so hold it back. The rich man "spares" his own animals, yet in verse 6 David condemns him because he "had no pity": the same verb, turned against him.

decisions.choice: a traveler: a guest who had to be fed
decisions.reason: Hospitality was a strict duty, and a guest was given a meal of meat (Genesis 18:1-8). The visitor is named three ways, "a traveler", "the wayfarer" and "the man who had come to him", but he is the same person.

decisions.choice: prepare: kill and cook for a meal
decisions.reason: "To make" or "prepare" an animal for a guest means to slaughter it and cook it (Genesis 18:7-8).

decisions.choice: did not want to (Balanced); visitor, guest (Balanced and Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "did not want to" for "spared", and use "visitor" and "guest" for the three names of the traveler so that it is clear one man is meant.

decisions.choice: One day; kill; make a meal; cooked
decisions.reason: Readable sets the scene with "One day" and spells out what preparing an animal for a guest involved (m3).

records.source: וַיִּֽחַר־אַ֥ף דָּוִ֛ד בָּאִ֖ישׁ מְאֹ֑ד וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל־נָתָ֔ן חַי־יְהוָ֕ה כִּ֣י בֶן־מָ֔וֶת הָאִ֖ישׁ הָעֹשֶׂ֥ה זֹֽאת׃
records.gloss: And burned [the] anger of David against the man very, and he said to Nathan, [as] lives Yahweh, surely a son of death [is] the man who did this.
pieces: David's anger burned hot against the man. "As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives," he said to Nathan, "the man who did this deserves to die!

L.5: And David's anger burned greatly against the man, and he said to Nathan, "[As] {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives, the man who did this [is] a son of death!

R.5: David became very angry with the rich man. "As surely as {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} lives," he told Nathan, "the man who did this should die!

decisions.choice: as the LORD lives: a solemn oath
decisions.reason: David swears by the life of Yahweh, which binds him to his own verdict (1 Samuel 14:39; 20:3). Without knowing it, he passes sentence on himself under oath.

decisions.choice: a son of death: a man who deserves to die
decisions.reason: "Son of" with a quality means a person marked by it. "Son of death" is someone who deserves death or is doomed to it (1 Samuel 20:31; 26:16).

decisions.choice: a verdict beyond the law
decisions.reason: The law for stealing a sheep was repayment, not death (Exodus 21:37, numbered 22:1 in some Bibles), as David himself goes on to say in verse 6. His outburst shows how wicked the rich man's act seems to him. Some take "son of death" as a cry of contempt ("he deserves to die") rather than a legal sentence.

decisions.choice: deserves to die (Balanced); should die (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the meaning of the idiom (m2); Literal keeps "son of death".

records.source: וְאֶת־הַכִּבְשָׂ֖ה יְשַׁלֵּ֣ם אַרְבַּעְתָּ֑יִם עֵ֗קֶב אֲשֶׁ֤ר עָשָׂה֙ אֶת־הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֔ה וְעַ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא־חָמָֽל׃
records.gloss: And the ewe-lamb he shall repay fourfold, because that he did the thing the this and because that not he had pity.
pieces: He must pay back four times over for the lamb, because he did this and because he had no pity."

L.6: And he shall repay the ewe lamb fourfold, because he did this thing and because he had no pity."

R.6: He must pay the poor man back four lambs for the one he took, because he did this and showed no pity."

decisions.choice: repay fourfold: the penalty the law set for a stolen sheep
decisions.reason: Exodus 21:37 (numbered 22:1 in some Bibles) says that whoever steals a sheep and slaughters it must repay four sheep for it. David the judge applies the law exactly.

decisions.choice: fourfold, as the Hebrew text reads
decisions.reason: Most manuscripts of the ancient Greek translation read "sevenfold", a number used for full repayment in Proverbs 6:31. The Hebrew reading agrees with the law of Exodus 21:37 and is followed.

decisions.choice: fourfold: a number that may look ahead in David's story
decisions.reason: Readers have long noticed that four of David's sons die in what follows: the child (verse 18), Amnon (13:28-29), Absalom (18:14-15) and Adonijah (1 Kings 2:25). The text does not draw this link itself.

decisions.choice: he had no pity: the same verb as "spared" in verse 4
decisions.reason: The rich man was sparing with his own flock but had no pity on the poor man. The wordplay sharpens the charge.

decisions.choice: pay the poor man back four lambs for the one he took
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what "fourfold" means here.

records.source: וַיֹּ֧אמֶר נָתָ֛ן אֶל־דָּוִ֖ד אַתָּ֣ה הָאִ֑ישׁ כֹּה־אָמַ֨ר יְהוָ֜ה אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אָנֹכִ֞י מְשַׁחְתִּ֤יךָֽ לְמֶ֨לֶךְ֙ עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְאָנֹכִ֥י הִצַּלְתִּ֖יךָ מִיַּ֥ד שָׁאֽוּל׃
records.gloss: And said Nathan to David, you [are] the man! Thus says Yahweh [the] God of Israel, I anointed you as king over Israel, and I delivered you from [the] hand of Saul.
pieces: Nathan said to David, "You are the man! {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, says this: 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I rescued you from Saul's power.

L.7: And Nathan said to David, "You [are] the man! Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel: 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I delivered you from the hand of Saul.

R.7: Then Nathan said to David, "You are that man! And this is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, says: 'I am the one who anointed you to be king over Israel, and I rescued you from Saul.

decisions.choice: You are the man: the verdict turns on the judge
decisions.reason: In Hebrew these are two short words, "you the man". David has just condemned "the man who did this" (verse 5); Nathan's reply applies that verdict to him.

decisions.choice: I ... I: God stresses that he himself acted
decisions.reason: The Hebrew adds the pronoun "I" before each verb, which it does not need. The emphasis falls on what God, not David, had done: everything David has, he received.

decisions.choice: I anointed you ... I delivered you: the story of 1 Samuel
decisions.reason: Samuel anointed David at God's command (1 Samuel 16:12-13), and God kept him safe through the years when Saul hunted him (1 Samuel 19-26).

decisions.choice: rescued you from Saul's power (Balanced); rescued you from Saul (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Hand" stands for power; Balanced says "power" and Readable leaves the picture out. Readable shows the emphatic "I" of m2 with "I am the one who".

decisions.choice: single quotes for God's words inside Nathan's speech
decisions.reason: The words Nathan reports from God are set in single quotes inside his own speech. They run to the end of verse 10; verse 11 opens a second saying of God, which runs to the end of verse 12.

records.source: וָאֶתְּנָ֨ה לְךָ֜ אֶת־בֵּ֣ית אֲדֹנֶ֗יךָ וְאֶת־נְשֵׁ֤י אֲדֹנֶ֨יךָ֙ בְּחֵיקֶ֔ךָ וָאֶתְּנָ֣ה לְךָ֔ אֶת־בֵּ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִֽיהוּדָ֑ה וְאִ֨ם־מְעָ֔ט וְאֹסִ֥פָה לְּךָ֖ כָּהֵ֥נָּה וְכָהֵֽנָּה׃
records.gloss: And I gave to you [the] house of your master and [the] wives of your master into your bosom, and I gave to you [the] house of Israel and Judah; and if [that were] too little, then I would add to you like these and like these.
pieces: I gave you your master's house and placed your master's wives in your embrace. I gave you the house of Israel and Judah too. And had that been too little, I would have given you much more besides.

L.8: And I gave you your master's house, and your master's wives into your bosom, and I gave you the house of Israel and Judah. And if [that were] too little, I would have added to you as much again and as much again.

R.8: I gave you all that had belonged to your master Saul, and I put his wives into your arms. I gave you the people of Israel and Judah to rule. If that had not been enough, I would have given you much more.

decisions.choice: your master's house: Saul's household and property
decisions.reason: "House" here is Saul's royal household, with its property and lands (9:7-9). "The house of Israel and Judah" then names the two parts of the people David now rules (2:4; 5:1-5).

decisions.choice: your master's wives into your bosom: Saul's royal household passed to David
decisions.reason: A new king took over the household of the old one, and taking a king's wives was a claim to his throne (16:21-22; 1 Kings 2:22). The books do not record that David married any of Saul's wives; the words may mean that all of Saul's household was placed under David's authority. The phrase also prepares for the charge of verse 9: David, who was given so much, took the one wife of another man.

decisions.choice: like these and like these: as much again, and more
decisions.reason: The doubled phrase means "so much and so much more". God would have given David still more if he had asked.

decisions.choice: your master Saul; the people of Israel and Judah to rule
decisions.reason: Readable names Saul and explains "the house of Israel and Judah" as the people David was given to rule.

records.source: מַדּ֜וּעַ בָּזִ֣יתָ׀אֶת־דְּבַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה לַעֲשׂ֣וֹת הָרַע֮ בְּעֵינַי֒ אֵ֣ת אוּרִיָּ֤ה הַֽחִתִּי֙ הִכִּ֣יתָ בַחֶ֔רֶב וְאֶ֨ת־אִשְׁתּ֔וֹ לָקַ֥חְתָּ לְּךָ֖ לְאִשָּׁ֑ה וְאֹת֣וֹ הָרַ֔גְתָּ בְּחֶ֖רֶב בְּנֵ֥י עַמּֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: Why have you despised [the] word of Yahweh to do the evil in my eyes? Uriah the Hittite you struck down with the sword, and his wife you took for yourself as a wife, and him you killed with [the] sword of [the] sons of Ammon.
pieces: Why have you despised the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} by doing what is evil in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} sight? You struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife to be your wife. You killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.

L.9: Why have you despised the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, doing what [is] evil in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} eyes? Uriah the Hittite you struck down with the sword, and his wife you took to be your wife, and him you killed with the sword of the sons of Ammon.

R.9: Why have you treated the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} with contempt? Why have you done what is evil in {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} eyes? You struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife as your own. You used the swords of the Ammonites to kill him.

decisions.choice: in my eyes, the reading the scribes marked
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) read "in his eyes", meaning in Yahweh's eyes; the scribes marked "in my eyes" to be read aloud (qere), which fits God speaking. The sense is the same. It also answers 11:25, where David told Joab not to let the matter be "evil in your eyes", and 11:27, where it was evil in Yahweh's eyes.

decisions.choice: despised the word of the LORD: treated God's commands as worthless
decisions.reason: To "despise" is to treat something with contempt. The "word" here is what Yahweh had commanded, including "You shall not murder" and "You shall not commit adultery" (Exodus 20:13-14). In verse 10 the charge becomes sharper: David despised God himself.

decisions.choice: Uriah ... his wife ... him: each placed first for emphasis
decisions.reason: Each charge begins with its object, which the Hebrew word order sets first for weight: Uriah, his wife, and Uriah again. David used the enemy's sword to kill him (11:14-17).

decisions.choice: You struck down Uriah ... took his wife ... You killed him
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable put the objects in the usual English order; Literal keeps the Hebrew order (m3).

decisions.choice: treated ... with contempt; two questions
decisions.reason: Readable explains "despised" and splits the long question in two.

records.source: וְעַתָּ֗ה לֹא־תָס֥וּר חֶ֛רֶב מִבֵּיתְךָ֖ עַד־עוֹלָ֑ם עֵ֚קֶב כִּ֣י בְזִתָ֔נִי וַתִּקַּ֗ח אֶת־אֵ֨שֶׁת֙ אוּרִיָּ֣ה הַחִתִּ֔י לִהְי֥וֹת לְךָ֖ לְאִשָּֽׁה׃ס
records.gloss: And now not shall depart [the] sword from your house until forever, because you despised me and took [the] wife of Uriah the Hittite to be for you as a wife.
pieces: So now the sword will never depart from your house, because you despised {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.'

L.10: And now the sword shall not depart from your house forever, because you despised {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and took the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.'

R.10: So now violence and killing will never leave your family, because you treated {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} with contempt. You took the wife of Uriah the Hittite and made her your own.'

decisions.choice: the sword shall not depart from your house: violent death will stay in David's family
decisions.reason: As David killed Uriah by the sword, so the sword will strike his own house. The story goes on to show it: Amnon is murdered by Absalom (13:28-29), Absalom dies in battle against his father (18:14-15), and Adonijah is put to death (1 Kings 2:25).

decisions.choice: forever: for the generations to come
decisions.reason: The phrase means a long and lasting time, here the life of David's dynasty, not without end. It answers the promise of 7:13-16, that God's faithful love would not depart from David's house: that promise stands, but so does this judgment.

decisions.choice: you despised me: to despise God's word is to despise God
decisions.reason: Verse 9 said David despised Yahweh's word; here God says David despised him. The sin was not only against Uriah but against God himself (verse 13).

decisions.choice: violence and killing; your family
decisions.reason: Readable explains "the sword" and says "family" for "house".

records.source: כֹּ֣ה׀אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה הִנְנִי֩ מֵקִ֨ים עָלֶ֤יךָ רָעָה֙ מִבֵּיתֶ֔ךָ וְלָקַחְתִּ֤י אֶת־נָשֶׁ֨יךָ֙ לְעֵינֶ֔יךָ וְנָתַתִּ֖י לְרֵעֶ֑יךָ וְשָׁכַב֙ עִם־נָשֶׁ֔יךָ לְעֵינֵ֖י הַשֶּׁ֥מֶשׁ הַזֹּֽאת׃
records.gloss: Thus says Yahweh, behold, I [am] raising against you evil from your house, and I will take your wives before your eyes and give [them] to your neighbor, and he will lie with your wives in [the] eyes of the sun the this.
pieces: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: 'I am about to raise up disaster against you from within your own household. Before your eyes I will take your wives and give them to one who is close to you, and he will lie with your wives in broad daylight.

L.11: Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: 'Look, I am raising up evil against you out of your own house. And I will take your wives before your eyes and give [them] to your neighbor, and he will lie with your wives in the sight of this sun.

R.11: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: 'I am going to bring trouble on you from your own family. While you watch, I will take your wives and give them to another man, and he will sleep with them in the light of day.

decisions.choice: evil: harm, disaster
decisions.reason: The word can mean moral evil or harm that comes on someone. Here it is the harm God will bring, an answer to the evil David did (verse 9).

decisions.choice: your neighbor: another man, one close to you
decisions.reason: The word means a fellow or companion, anyone besides oneself (1 Samuel 15:28). The words "from your own house" show that it will be someone from David's own family.

decisions.choice: he will lie with your wives: fulfilled through Absalom
decisions.reason: When Absalom rebels, he lies with his father's concubines in a tent on the roof of the palace, in the sight of all Israel (16:21-22).

decisions.choice: in the eyes of this sun: openly, in broad daylight
decisions.reason: The sun is pictured as a witness that sees everything. What David did in secret (verse 12) will be paid back in the open.

decisions.choice: in broad daylight (Balanced); in the light of day (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the idiom (m4).

decisions.choice: another man; sleep with them
decisions.reason: Readable uses plain words for "your neighbor" and "lie with".

records.source: כִּ֥י אַתָּ֖ה עָשִׂ֣יתָ בַסָּ֑תֶר וַאֲנִ֗י אֶעֱשֶׂה֙ אֶת־הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֔ה נֶ֥גֶד כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וְנֶ֥גֶד הַשָּֽׁמֶשׁ׃ס
records.gloss: For you did [it] in secret, but I will do the thing the this before all Israel and before the sun.
pieces: You acted in secret, but I will do this in front of all Israel, in broad daylight.'"

L.12: For you acted in secret, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.'"

R.12: You sinned in secret, but I will do this openly, in front of all Israel and in broad daylight.'"

decisions.choice: you ... I: two emphatic pronouns set side by side
decisions.reason: The Hebrew places "you" and "I" in contrast: David hid his deed, but God will act in public.

decisions.choice: before the sun: openly
decisions.reason: As in verse 11, the sun stands for full daylight and public view.

decisions.choice: sinned; openly
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what David did in secret and adds "openly" to make the contrast clear.

decisions.choice: both quotations close
decisions.reason: God's second saying (single quotes) and Nathan's speech (double quotes) both end here.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר דָּוִד֙ אֶל־נָתָ֔ן חָטָ֖אתִי לַֽיהוָ֑הסוַיֹּ֨אמֶר נָתָ֜ן אֶל־דָּוִ֗ד גַּם־יְהוָ֛ה הֶעֱבִ֥יר חַטָּאתְךָ֖ לֹ֥א תָמֽוּת׃
records.gloss: And said David to Nathan, I have sinned against Yahweh. And said Nathan to David, also Yahweh has caused to pass away your sin; not you will die.
pieces: David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}." Nathan said to David, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has taken away your sin. You will not die.

L.13: And David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}." And Nathan said to David, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} also has put away your sin; you shall not die.

R.13: Then David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}." Nathan answered, "{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} has taken away your sin. You will not die.

decisions.choice: I have sinned against the LORD: a confession without excuse
decisions.reason: David makes no defense. He names his sin as sin against Yahweh himself, though Uriah and Bathsheba were the ones wronged (compare Psalm 51:6). The title of Psalm 51 (Hebrew 51:1-2) links that psalm to this moment.

decisions.choice: has put away your sin: has removed it, forgiven it
decisions.reason: The verb means to make something pass over or pass away. Yahweh takes the guilt away from David (24:10; Job 7:21).

decisions.choice: also: on his part
decisions.reason: The small word "also" answers David's confession: David has confessed, and Yahweh for his part has removed the sin. It can also simply add weight ("indeed").

decisions.choice: you will not die: the death David deserved is not carried out
decisions.reason: Under the law adultery and murder were both punished by death (Leviticus 20:10; Numbers 35:31). David had also spoken the sentence "son of death" over the man in the story (verse 5).

decisions.choice: has taken away (Balanced and Readable, without "also")
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable leave out "also", whose force English carries by the order of the two speeches (m3); Literal keeps it.

decisions.choice: Nathan's speech continues into verse 14
decisions.reason: Nathan's answer runs on into the next verse, so its quotation closes there.

records.heading: David admits his sin

records.source: אֶ֗פֶס כִּֽי־נִאֵ֤ץ נִאַ֨צְתָּ֙ אֶת־אֹיְבֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה בַּדָּבָ֖ר הַזֶּ֑ה גַּ֗ם הַבֵּ֛ן הַיִּלּ֥וֹד לְךָ֖ מ֥וֹת יָמֽוּת׃
records.gloss: Nevertheless, because utterly you have scorned [the] enemies of Yahweh by the thing the this, also the son the born to you surely will die.
pieces: But because by doing this you have given the enemies of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} every reason to scorn {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, the son who has been born to you will surely die."

L.14: Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly given the enemies of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} cause to scorn, the son who is born to you shall also surely die."

R.14: But by doing this you have caused the enemies of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to look down on {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. So the son who has been born to you will die."

decisions.choice: the enemies of the LORD, as the Hebrew text reads
alternatives: you have utterly scorned the LORD (the probable earlier wording)
decisions.reason: The words "the enemies of" were probably added by scribes so that the text would not say outright that David scorned Yahweh. Scribes softened other places where a curse or insult would fall on God or his chosen king in the same way (compare 1 Samuel 25:22, "the enemies of David"). Without the added words the sentence reads "you have utterly scorned Yahweh". The Hebrew text is followed, but its sense is that David's deed was contempt for Yahweh himself, as verses 9-10 have said.

decisions.choice: you have utterly given cause to scorn
decisions.reason: The verb is doubled for emphasis. With "the enemies of Yahweh" as its object, it is read here as "made them scorn": David's deed has given God's enemies reason to despise him. Elsewhere the same form means simply "scorn" (Isaiah 1:4), and that is its sense if the words "the enemies of" are a later softening (m1).

decisions.choice: the son will die: forgiveness does not undo every consequence
decisions.reason: David himself will not die (verse 13), but the child born from his adultery will. The judgment of the sword on his house (verse 10) also still stands.

decisions.choice: nevertheless, because: a turn after forgiveness
decisions.reason: The opening word limits what was just said: the sin is put away, but something remains.

decisions.choice: every reason to scorn him (Balanced); to look down on him (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply "him", the one scorned, which the reading of m2 implies; Literal leaves it unexpressed.

decisions.choice: two sentences joined by "So"
decisions.reason: Readable splits the verse and states the cause first.

records.source: וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ נָתָ֖ן אֶל־בֵּית֑וֹ וַיִּגֹּ֣ף יְהוָ֗ה אֶת־הַיֶּ֜לֶד אֲשֶׁ֨ר יָלְדָ֧ה אֵֽשֶׁת־אוּרִיָּ֛ה לְדָוִ֖ד וַיֵּאָנַֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: And went Nathan to his house. And struck Yahweh the child that had borne [the] wife of Uriah to David, and he became sick.
pieces: After Nathan had gone home, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} struck the child whom Uriah's wife had borne to David, and the boy fell gravely ill.

L.15: And Nathan went to his house. And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} struck the child that the wife of Uriah had borne to David, and he became very sick.

R.15: Then Nathan went back home. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} struck the baby that Uriah's wife had borne to David, and the baby became very sick.

decisions.choice: the wife of Uriah: the narrator still names her by her husband
decisions.reason: The child's mother is called "the wife of Uriah", not "David's wife", keeping the wrong in view. Only after the child's death, in verse 24, is she named Bathsheba, David's wife.

decisions.choice: became very sick: fell seriously, hopelessly ill
decisions.reason: The verb is used of a wound or sickness that cannot be cured (Jeremiah 17:9; Micah 1:9; Job 34:6).

decisions.choice: the LORD struck the child
decisions.reason: The illness is presented as God's act, carrying out the word of verse 14.

decisions.choice: he (not "it") for the child
decisions.reason: The child is the son of verse 14, so a personal pronoun is used. Readable repeats "the baby" for clarity.

records.source: וַיְבַקֵּ֥שׁ דָּוִ֛ד אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים בְּעַ֣ד הַנָּ֑עַר וַיָּ֤צָם דָּוִד֙ צ֔וֹם וּבָ֥א וְלָ֖ן וְשָׁכַ֥ב אָֽרְצָה׃
records.gloss: And sought David the God for the boy, and fasted David a fast, and went in and spent the night and lay [on the] ground.
pieces: David pleaded with God for the boy. He fasted, and he went in and spent the nights lying on the ground.

L.16: And David sought God for the boy, and David fasted a fast, and he would go in and spend the night lying on the ground.

R.16: David begged God to save the boy. He would not eat anything. He went inside and spent each night lying on the ground.

decisions.choice: sought God for the boy: pleaded with God for the child's life
decisions.reason: To "seek" God here is to ask for his favor in prayer (21:1). David pleads, even after Nathan's word, in the hope that God may yet relent (verse 22).

decisions.choice: went in, spent the night, lay: again and again
decisions.reason: These verb forms describe what David did repeatedly over the days of the illness, not on one night only.

decisions.choice: fasting and lying on the ground: signs of grief and humbling oneself
decisions.reason: Going without food and lying on the bare ground were ways of mourning and of pleading before God (13:31; 1 Kings 21:27). Where David went "in" to is not said; it may have been an inner room of his house.

decisions.choice: pleaded with (Balanced); begged ... to save (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Sought" is given its sense here (m1).

decisions.choice: would not eat anything
decisions.reason: Readable says what fasting meant.

records.source: וַיָּקֻ֜מוּ זִקְנֵ֤י בֵיתוֹ֙ עָלָ֔יו לַהֲקִימ֖וֹ מִן־הָאָ֑רֶץ וְלֹ֣א אָבָ֔ה וְלֹֽא־בָרָ֥א אִתָּ֖ם לָֽחֶם׃
records.gloss: And stood up [the] elders of his house over him to raise him from the ground, and not he was willing, and not he ate with them food.
pieces: The elders of his household stood beside him to get him up from the ground, but he refused, and he would not eat any food with them.

L.17: And the elders of his house stood over him to raise him from the ground, but he was not willing, and he did not eat food with them.

R.17: The older men who served in his household stood around him and tried to get him up off the ground. But he refused, and he would not eat with them.

decisions.choice: the elders of his house: the senior members of the royal household
decisions.reason: These were the older, trusted men of the king's household, its leading servants and advisers (Genesis 24:2; 50:7).

decisions.choice: ate: took food
decisions.reason: The verb used here is a less common word for eating, used also of food given to the sick and mourning (13:5-6, 10).

decisions.choice: the older men who served in his household
decisions.reason: Readable explains "elders of his house" (m1).

records.source: וַיְהִ֛י בַּיּ֥וֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִ֖י וַיָּ֣מָת הַיָּ֑לֶד וַיִּֽרְאוּ֩ עַבְדֵ֨י דָוִ֜ד לְהַגִּ֥יד ל֣וֹ׀כִּי־מֵ֣ת הַיֶּ֗לֶד כִּ֤י אָֽמְרוּ֙ הִנֵּה֩ בִהְי֨וֹת הַיֶּ֜לֶד חַ֗י דִּבַּ֤רְנוּ אֵלָיו֙ וְלֹא־שָׁמַ֣ע בְּקוֹלֵ֔נוּ וְאֵ֨יךְ נֹאמַ֥ר אֵלָ֛יו מֵ֥ת הַיֶּ֖לֶד וְעָשָׂ֥ה רָעָֽה׃
records.gloss: And it was on the day the seventh, and died the child. And feared [the] servants of David to tell him that had died the child, for they said, behold, while the child was alive we spoke to him and not he listened to our voice; and how will we say to him, has died the child? And he will do harm.
pieces: The child died on the seventh day, and David's servants were afraid to give him the news. They said, "While the child was still living, we spoke to him and he paid no attention to us. How can we tell him the child is dead? He may do something harmful."

L.18: And it happened on the seventh day that the child died. And David's servants were afraid to tell him that the child had died, for they said, "Look, while the child was alive we spoke to him, and he did not listen to our voice. And how can we say to him, 'The child has died'? He will do harm."

R.18: The child died on the seventh day. David's servants were afraid to tell him. They said, "While the child was still alive, we talked to David, but he would not listen to us. How can we tell him that the child has died? He might do something terrible."

decisions.choice: the seventh day: probably of the illness
alternatives: the seventh day of the child's life
decisions.reason: The day is counted from the start of the illness (verse 15) or of David's fast, most likely. If it were the child's age, he would have died before the eighth day, when a boy was circumcised and named (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3); the text gives him no name.

decisions.choice: David's servants: the attendants of his household
decisions.reason: These are the king's household servants and officials who were with him through the fast, among them the elders of verse 17.

decisions.choice: he will do harm: to himself or to others
decisions.reason: The words do not say whom David might harm. The servants fear that a grief so great before the death will become something worse after it.

decisions.choice: servants at every level
decisions.reason: These are the king's household attendants, not officials sent out on his business, so "servants" is used at every level, as for the king's servants in 1 Samuel.

decisions.choice: talked to David
decisions.reason: Readable names David, since "him" might seem to point to the child.

records.source: וַיַּ֣רְא דָּוִ֗ד כִּ֤י עֲבָדָיו֙ מִֽתְלַחֲשִׁ֔ים וַיָּ֥בֶן דָּוִ֖ד כִּ֣י מֵ֣ת הַיָּ֑לֶד וַיֹּ֨אמֶר דָּוִ֧ד אֶל־עֲבָדָ֛יו הֲמֵ֥ת הַיֶּ֖לֶד וַיֹּ֥אמְרוּ מֵֽת׃
records.gloss: And saw David that his servants were whispering to one another, and understood David that had died the child; and said David to his servants, has died the child? And they said, he has died.
pieces: When David saw his servants whispering to one another, he realized that the child was dead. So he asked his servants, "Has the child died?" They answered, "He has died."

L.19: And David saw that his servants were whispering together, and David understood that the child had died. And David said to his servants, "Has the child died?" And they said, "He has died."

R.19: But David saw his servants whispering to each other, and he understood that the child had died. "Is the child dead?" he asked them. "Yes, he is dead," they answered.

decisions.choice: He has died: an answer of yes
decisions.reason: Hebrew answers a question by repeating its verb. The servants' one-word reply confirms the death.

decisions.choice: When David saw ..., he realized
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable join the first two clauses and do not repeat David's name three times.

decisions.choice: Yes
decisions.reason: Readable adds "Yes" to show that the reply answers the question (m1).

records.source: וַיָּקָם֩ דָּוִ֨ד מֵהָאָ֜רֶץ וַיִּרְחַ֣ץ וַיָּ֗סֶךְ וַיְחַלֵּף֙ שִׂמְלֹתָ֔יו וַיָּבֹ֥א בֵית־יְהוָ֖ה וַיִּשְׁתָּ֑חוּ וַיָּבֹא֙ אֶל־בֵּית֔וֹ וַיִּשְׁאַ֕ל וַיָּשִׂ֥ימוּ ל֛וֹ לֶ֖חֶם וַיֹּאכַֽל׃
records.gloss: And arose David from the ground and washed and anointed [himself] and changed his garments and came [to the] house of Yahweh and bowed down; and came to his house and asked, and they set for him food and he ate.
pieces: Then David got up from the ground. He washed, put oil on himself and changed his clothes. He entered the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and bowed in worship. After that he went to his own house and asked for food, and when they set it before him, he ate.

L.20: And David arose from the ground and washed and anointed [himself] and changed his clothes, and he went into the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and bowed down. Then he came to his own house and asked, and they set food before him, and he ate.

R.20: Then David got up from the ground. He washed himself, put olive oil on his skin and changed his clothes. He went to the house of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to worship. After that he went home and asked for something to eat. They served him food, and he ate.

decisions.choice: washed, anointed himself, changed his clothes: the end of mourning
decisions.reason: Rubbing oil into the skin was part of normal grooming, and people in mourning left it off (14:2; Ruth 3:3). By washing, oiling himself and putting on fresh clothes, David shows that his time of pleading and grief is over.

decisions.choice: the house of the LORD: the tent where the ark stood
decisions.reason: The temple had not yet been built (7:1-13). The "house of Yahweh" here is the tent David had pitched for the ark in Jerusalem (6:17).

decisions.choice: bowed down: worshiped
decisions.reason: The verb means to bow down to the ground, the posture of worship. David accepts God's verdict and worships.

decisions.choice: his clothes, the reading the scribes marked
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) can be read as a singular, "his garment"; the reading marked to be read aloud (qere) is plural, "his clothes". The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: put oil on himself (Balanced); put olive oil on his skin (Readable)
decisions.reason: "Anointed" here is a matter of grooming, not of anointing for an office, so Balanced and Readable describe it plainly.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֤וּ עֲבָדָיו֙ אֵלָ֔יו מָֽה־הַדָּבָ֥ר הַזֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשִׂ֑יתָה בַּעֲב֞וּר הַיֶּ֤לֶד חַי֙ צַ֣מְתָּ וַתֵּ֔בְךְּ וְכַֽאֲשֶׁר֙ מֵ֣ת הַיֶּ֔לֶד קַ֖מְתָּ וַתֹּ֥אכַל לָֽחֶם׃
records.gloss: And said his servants to him, what [is] the thing the this that you have done? For the sake of the child [while] alive you fasted and wept, and when died the child you arose and ate food.
pieces: His servants said to him, "What is this you have done? While the child was alive, you fasted and wept for him, but now that the child is dead, you get up and eat!"

L.21: And his servants said to him, "What [is] this thing that you have done? For the sake of the living child you fasted and wept, but when the child died, you arose and ate food."

R.21: His servants asked him, "Why are you acting like this? When the child was alive, you would not eat, and you cried for him. But now that he is dead, you get up and eat!"

decisions.choice: fasting before the death, eating after it: the reverse of custom
decisions.reason: People fasted after a death, as a sign of mourning (1 Samuel 31:13; 2 Samuel 1:12; 3:35). David did the opposite, and his servants cannot understand it.

decisions.choice: for the sake of the living child: while he was alive
alternatives: while the child was still alive (the ancient Greek translation)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "for the sake of the child, alive". The ancient Greek translation reads "while the child was still alive", as in verse 22. Either way the sense is that David fasted for the child while there was still hope.

decisions.choice: Why are you acting like this?
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the servants' question, which asks for a reason rather than a description.

records.source: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר בְּעוֹד֙ הַיֶּ֣לֶד חַ֔י צַ֖מְתִּי וָֽאֶבְכֶּ֑ה כִּ֤י אָמַ֨רְתִּי֙ מִ֣י יוֹדֵ֔עַ וְחַנַּ֥נִי יְהוָ֖ה וְחַ֥י הַיָּֽלֶד׃
records.gloss: And he said, while still the child [was] alive I fasted and wept, for I said, who knows? And will be gracious to me Yahweh and will live the child.
pieces: He said, "While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept. I thought, 'Who knows? {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} may be gracious to me and let the child live.'

L.22: And he said, "While the child was still alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, 'Who knows? {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} may be gracious to me, and the child may live.'

R.22: David answered, "While the child was still alive, I would not eat, and I cried. I thought, 'Maybe {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will be kind to me and let the child live.'

decisions.choice: who knows?: a hope that God may still relent
decisions.reason: The question expresses hope, not certainty, that God in his freedom may change what he has said (Joel 2:14; Jonah 3:9).

decisions.choice: be gracious to me: show me favor
decisions.reason: The verb means to show undeserved kindness, here by sparing the child.

decisions.choice: and he will be gracious, the reading the scribes marked
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) and the reading marked to be read aloud (qere) differ only in a small connecting letter at the start of the verb. The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: I said: I thought
decisions.reason: "Said" here means said to oneself, that is, thought.

decisions.choice: I thought
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of "I said" (m4).

decisions.choice: Maybe; be kind to me
decisions.reason: Readable turns the question "Who knows?" into "Maybe" and uses "kind" for "gracious".

records.source: וְעַתָּ֣ה׀מֵ֗ת לָ֤מָּה זֶּה֙ אֲנִ֣י צָ֔ם הַאוּכַ֥ל לַהֲשִׁיב֖וֹ ע֑וֹד אֲנִי֙ הֹלֵ֣ךְ אֵלָ֔יו וְה֖וּא לֹֽא־יָשׁ֥וּב אֵלָֽי׃
records.gloss: And now he has died; why this [am] I fasting? Am I able to bring him back again? I [am] going to him, and he not will return to me.
pieces: But now he has died. Why should I go on fasting? Am I able to bring him back? I will go to him one day, but he will not come back to me."

L.23: But now he has died. Why [am] I fasting? Am I able to bring him back again? I am going to him, but he will not return to me."

R.23: But now he is dead. Why should I go without food? I cannot bring him back again. Someday I will go to where he is, but he cannot come back to me."

decisions.choice: I am going to him: I too will die
decisions.reason: David will one day go where the child has gone, to death and the place of the dead (Genesis 37:35). The words show acceptance of death's finality; they do not describe what that place is like.

decisions.choice: Am I able to bring him back?: a question expecting the answer no
decisions.reason: David asks the question to say that nothing he does can bring the child back.

decisions.choice: I cannot bring him back again
decisions.reason: Readable states the answer to David's question directly (m2).

decisions.choice: Someday; to where he is
decisions.reason: Readable makes it clear that David means his own death.

records.source: וַיְנַחֵ֣ם דָּוִ֗ד אֵ֚ת בַּת־שֶׁ֣בַע אִשְׁתּ֔וֹ וַיָּבֹ֥א אֵלֶ֖יהָ וַיִּשְׁכַּ֣ב עִמָּ֑הּ וַתֵּ֣לֶד בֵּ֗ן וַתִּקְרָ֤א אֶת־שְׁמוֹ֙ שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה וַיהוָ֖ה אֲהֵבֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: And comforted David Bathsheba his wife, and went to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and she called his name Solomon; and Yahweh loved him,
pieces: Then David comforted his wife Bathsheba. He went to her and slept with her, and she gave birth to a son, and she named him Solomon. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} loved him,

L.24: And David comforted Bathsheba his wife, and he went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and she called his name Solomon. And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} loved him,

R.24: Then David comforted his wife Bathsheba. He slept with her, and she became pregnant and had a son. She named him Solomon. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} loved the boy.

decisions.choice: she called his name, the reading the scribes marked
alternatives: he called his name (the written consonants)
decisions.reason: The written consonants (ketiv) read "he called", that is, David named the boy; the scribes marked "she called" to be read aloud (qere), so that Bathsheba names him. Mothers often named their children (Genesis 29:32-35; 1 Samuel 1:20). The marked reading is followed.

decisions.choice: Solomon: a name linked with peace and wholeness
decisions.reason: The name sounds like the word for peace and wholeness (*shalom*), and Solomon's reign was a time of peace (1 Chronicles 22:9). It may also be heard as "his replacement", from a related verb meaning to make good a loss, since he is born after the child who died.

decisions.choice: Bathsheba his wife: now named and called David's wife
decisions.reason: Since chapter 11 she has been "the wife of Uriah" (verse 15). Now the narrator gives her name and calls her David's wife. David comforts her: she too had lost her child.

decisions.choice: the LORD loved him: God's favor on Solomon from birth
decisions.reason: God's love marks Solomon out from the beginning, and leads to the name given in verse 25 (compare 7:12-15).

decisions.choice: became pregnant and had a son; the boy
decisions.reason: Readable fills the step between the two acts and names the one loved as the boy, so that "him" is not taken for David.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֗ח בְּיַד֙ נָתָ֣ן הַנָּבִ֔יא וַיִּקְרָ֥א אֶת־שְׁמ֖וֹ יְדִ֣ידְיָ֑הּ בַּעֲב֖וּר יְהוָֽה׃פ
records.gloss: and he sent by [the] hand of Nathan the prophet, and he called his name Jedidiah, for the sake of Yahweh.
pieces: and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent word through Nathan the prophet, and he named him Jedidiah because of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.25: and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, and he called his name Jedidiah, because of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.25: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} sent a message through Nathan the prophet, and the boy was named Jedidiah, which means "loved by {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}". This name was given because of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: he sent ... he called: the LORD sent word, and the name came from him
decisions.reason: The one who sends is most naturally Yahweh, who has just been said to love the child (verse 24). He sends a message through Nathan, and the name is given at his word, whether Nathan or David was the one who spoke it.

decisions.choice: Jedidiah: "beloved of the LORD"
decisions.reason: The name joins a word meaning "beloved" with a short form of the divine name. It repeats what verse 24 says, that Yahweh loved him. The word for "beloved" also sounds like the name David.

decisions.choice: a second name
decisions.reason: Solomon is never called Jedidiah again. The name is a sign of God's favor rather than the name he was known by.

decisions.choice: because of the LORD: for the LORD's sake, as the LORD willed
alternatives: by the word of the LORD (the ancient Greek translation)
decisions.reason: The phrase gives the reason for the name: it came from Yahweh and expresses his love. The ancient Greek translation reads "by the word of the Lord", which comes to much the same.

decisions.choice: The LORD sent a message ... the boy was named
decisions.reason: Readable starts a new sentence with the subject named, and uses "was named" so that it does not decide who spoke the name (m1). It explains the name's meaning in words, not as a quotation.

records.source: וַיִּלָּ֣חֶם יוֹאָ֔ב בְּרַבַּ֖ת בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֑וֹן וַיִּלְכֹּ֖ד אֶת־עִ֥יר הַמְּלוּכָֽה׃
records.gloss: And fought Joab against Rabbah of [the] sons of Ammon and captured the city of the kingship.
pieces: Meanwhile Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and took the royal city.

L.26: And Joab fought against Rabbah of the sons of Ammon and captured the royal city.

R.26: Meanwhile Joab was fighting against Rabbah, the capital of the Ammonites, and he captured the king's part of the city.

decisions.choice: the war with Ammon again: the story returns to 11:1
decisions.reason: The siege of Rabbah began in 11:1, while David stayed in Jerusalem. The writer now finishes that account. These events may have happened during the time of verses 15-25 or before them; the text does not give their order in time.

decisions.choice: Rabbah: the capital of the Ammonites
decisions.reason: Rabbah stood east of the Jordan, where the city of Amman is today (Deuteronomy 3:11).

decisions.choice: the royal city: the king's quarter or stronghold
decisions.reason: The phrase seems to name a part of Rabbah, since Joab says in verse 28 that the city itself has still to be taken. It may be the same part he calls "the city of waters" in verse 27.

decisions.choice: Meanwhile
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable add "Meanwhile" to mark the return to the war (m1).

decisions.choice: the capital of the Ammonites; the king's part of the city
decisions.reason: Readable explains who the people of Rabbah were and what "the royal city" was.

records.heading: Rabbah is captured

records.source: וַיִּשְׁלַ֥ח יוֹאָ֛ב מַלְאָכִ֖ים אֶל־דָּוִ֑ד וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ נִלְחַ֣מְתִּי בְרַבָּ֔ה גַּם־לָכַ֖דְתִּי אֶת־עִ֥יר הַמָּֽיִם׃
records.gloss: And sent Joab messengers to David and said, I have fought against Rabbah; also I have captured [the] city of the waters.
pieces: Joab sent messengers to tell David, "I have fought against Rabbah, and I have taken the city's water supply.

L.27: And Joab sent messengers to David and said, "I have fought against Rabbah; I have also captured the city of waters.

R.27: Joab sent messengers to David to tell him, "I have attacked Rabbah, and I have captured the place where the city gets its water.

decisions.choice: the city of waters: the part of Rabbah that held its water supply
alternatives: the lower city by the river
decisions.reason: This was probably the lower town by the stream, where the city's water came from, or a fortified water source. Once it was taken, the citadel above could not hold out for long.

decisions.choice: the city's water supply (Balanced); the place where the city gets its water (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "the city of waters" was (m1).

records.source: וְעַתָּ֗ה אֱסֹף֙ אֶת־יֶ֣תֶר הָעָ֔ם וַחֲנֵ֥ה עַל־הָעִ֖יר וְלָכְדָ֑הּ פֶּן־אֶלְכֹּ֤ד אֲנִי֙ אֶת־הָעִ֔יר וְנִקְרָ֥א שְׁמִ֖י עָלֶֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: And now, gather [the] rest of the people and encamp against the city and capture it, lest I capture I the city and be called my name over it.
pieces: Now gather the rest of the troops, camp against the city and capture it. Otherwise I will capture the city myself, and it will be named after me."

L.28: And now, gather the rest of the people and encamp against the city and capture it, lest I myself capture the city and my name be called over it."

R.28: Now bring the rest of the army together. Surround the city and capture it yourself. If you do not, I will capture it, and people will call it by my name."

decisions.choice: the people: the fighting men
decisions.reason: "The people" here means the army in the field, the men not yet sent out with Joab.

decisions.choice: my name be called over it: it would be counted as mine
decisions.reason: To have one's name called over something was to claim it as one's own (Isaiah 4:1; Amos 9:12). Joab wants the king to take the credit for the victory.

decisions.choice: I myself: the pronoun is added for emphasis
decisions.reason: The Hebrew adds "I" after the verb, stressing that Joab, not David, would then be the conqueror.

decisions.choice: the troops (Balanced); the army (Readable)
decisions.reason: As elsewhere in Samuel, "the people" meaning the army is "the troops" at Balanced and "the army" at Readable; Literal keeps "the people".

decisions.choice: yourself
decisions.reason: Readable adds "yourself" to show the point of Joab's request.

records.source: וַיֶּאֱסֹ֥ף דָּוִ֛ד אֶת־כָּל־הָעָ֖ם וַיֵּ֣לֶךְ רַבָּ֑תָה וַיִּלָּ֥חֶם בָּ֖הּ וַֽיִּלְכְּדָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: And gathered David all the people and went to Rabbah and fought against it and captured it.
pieces: So David gathered all the troops and went to Rabbah. He fought against it and captured it.

L.29: And David gathered all the people and went to Rabbah and fought against it and captured it.

R.29: So David gathered the whole army and went to Rabbah. He attacked the city and captured it.

decisions.choice: David goes to the war
decisions.reason: In 11:1 David stayed in Jerusalem while the army went to Rabbah; now he goes out himself and leads the final attack.

decisions.choice: troops (Balanced); army (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 28.

records.source: וַיִּקַּ֣ח אֶת־עֲטֶֽרֶת־מַלְכָּם֩ מֵעַ֨ל רֹאשׁ֜וֹ וּמִשְׁקָלָ֨הּ כִּכַּ֤ר זָהָב֙ וְאֶ֣בֶן יְקָרָ֔ה וַתְּהִ֖י עַל־רֹ֣אשׁ דָּוִ֑ד וּשְׁלַ֥ל הָעִ֛יר הוֹצִ֖יא הַרְבֵּ֥ה מְאֹֽד׃
records.gloss: And he took [the] crown of their king from upon his head, and its weight [was a] talent of gold and precious stone, and it was on [the] head of David; and [the] plunder of the city he brought out, much very.
pieces: He took the crown from their king's head. It weighed {{units:about 75 pounds|a talent}} of gold and held a precious stone, and it was placed on David's head. He also brought a great amount of plunder out of the city.

L.30: And he took the crown of their king from his head, and its weight [was] a talent of gold, and [it had] a precious stone; and it was [set] on David's head. And he brought out the plunder of the city, very much.

R.30: David took the crown off the head of the Ammonite king. It was made of gold weighing {{units:about 75 pounds|a talent}}, and it had a precious jewel in it. It was placed on David's head. David also took a huge amount of valuable things from the city.

decisions.choice: their king
alternatives: Milcom, the god of the Ammonites
decisions.reason: The same letters can be read as "Milcom", the name of the Ammonite god (1 Kings 11:5, 33), and the ancient Greek translation reads "Milcom their king". A crown so heavy would suit the statue of a god better than a man's head. The Hebrew vowels read "their king", which is followed here.

decisions.choice: a talent of gold: a very heavy weight
decisions.reason: A talent was the largest unit of weight, about 75 pounds. A crown of that weight could have been worn only briefly, on a ceremonial occasion.

decisions.choice: it was on David's head: the crown, or perhaps the stone
decisions.reason: The words "it was" could refer to the crown or to the precious stone; if the stone, it was set into David's own crown. 1 Chronicles 20:2 tells this in almost the same words.

decisions.choice: about 75 pounds (a talent)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the modern weight, with the original unit as the alternative; Literal keeps "talent".

decisions.choice: the Ammonite king; valuable things
decisions.reason: Readable names whose king is meant and says what plunder was.

records.source: וְאֶת־הָעָ֨ם אֲשֶׁר־בָּ֜הּ הוֹצִ֗יא וַיָּ֣שֶׂם בַּ֠מְּגֵרָה וּבַחֲרִצֵ֨י הַבַּרְזֶ֜ל וּֽבְמַגְזְרֹ֣ת הַבַּרְזֶ֗ל וְהֶעֱבִ֤יר אוֹתָם֙ בַּמַּלְבֵּ֔ן וְכֵ֣ן יַעֲשֶׂ֔ה לְכֹ֖ל עָרֵ֣י בְנֵֽי־עַמּ֑וֹן וַיָּ֧שָׁב דָּוִ֛ד וְכָל־הָעָ֖ם יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם׃פ
records.gloss: And the people who [were] in it he brought out and set [them] to the saw and to [the] picks of the iron and to [the] axes of the iron, and made pass them through the brick-mold; and thus he did to all [the] cities of [the] sons of Ammon. And returned David and all the people [to] Jerusalem.
pieces: He brought out the people who were in the city and put them to work with saws, iron picks and iron axes, and he made them labor at the brick molds. He did the same to all the towns of the Ammonites. Then David and all the troops returned to Jerusalem.

L.31: And he brought out the people who [were] in it and set [them] to the saw and to iron picks and to iron axes, and made them pass through the brick mold. And thus he did to all the cities of the sons of Ammon. And David and all the people returned [to] Jerusalem.

R.31: He brought out the people who lived in the city and forced them to work with saws, iron picks and iron axes, and to make bricks. He did the same to all the Ammonite towns. Then David and the whole army went back to Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: set them to saws, picks and axes: put them to forced labor
alternatives: put them under saws, picks and axes, killing them
decisions.reason: The words "set at" with tools most naturally mean that the people were made to work with them, as conquered peoples were put to forced labor (Joshua 9:21-27; 1 Kings 9:20-21). An older reading takes the verse to mean that David had them cut to pieces with these tools. That reading leans on the parallel in 1 Chronicles 20:3, which has a verb that can mean "he sawed"; it differs from "he set" by one letter and is often thought to be a copying slip. The forced-labor reading is followed, but the matter is not certain.

decisions.choice: made them pass through the brick mold, the reading the scribes marked
alternatives: made them pass through Malken (the written consonants)
decisions.reason: The scribes marked "brick mold" or "brickworks" to be read aloud (qere), meaning work at making bricks. The written consonants (ketiv) are hard to explain; some connect them with the Ammonite god Milcom (verse 30), since "make pass through" is the phrase used for passing children through the fire to a god (2 Kings 16:3; 23:10). The marked reading is followed, in line with m1.

decisions.choice: all the people: the army
decisions.reason: In the last sentence "the people" are again David's troops (verse 29), returning home with him.

decisions.choice: put them to work with (Balanced); forced them to work with, and to make bricks (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable state the reading chosen in m1 and m2; Literal keeps the bare Hebrew phrases "set to" and "made pass through".

decisions.choice: the troops (Balanced); the whole army (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 28.
